newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota chief warns it leaning away from Britain.
newsitem.headline: Toyota chief warns it leaning away from Britain.

text.p: Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda on Wednesday seemed to rule out any investment in the near future by the carmaker in Britain, and warned that the company would turn all its attention to the continent if London stayed out of European monetary union.

In comments that could turn into an issue in Britain's upcoming general election campaign, Okuda left no doubt that a Britain outside the European Economic and Monetary union (EMU) was of little interest to the giant carmaker.
"Regardless on whether Britain joins (the EMU), I have a feeling that it would be excessive if we made additional (investments) in Britain," Okuda told reporters.
Okuda said that Toyota would shift its European investments to continental Europe if Britain did not join the EMU.
Asked if Toyota's future strategy in Britain will change depending on whether that country joins the EMU, Okuda said, "It will change."
Toyota last year built 117,000 cars at its plant in Derbyshire, central England, and is considering how rapidly to expand production there.

Last week, Britain's main opposition Labour party seized on less forthright comments by a senior Toyota European executive that Toyota was worried that some Conservative "Euro-sceptics" wanted to pull out of the European Union.
"It would be of great concern to Toyota if the UK found itself excluded from the European Union," Alan Marsh, vice-chairman of Toyota Motor Europe, told the Times newspaper.

Labour leader Tony Blair, referring to the Toyota report, said in a pre-election pep talk to his party: "People know that Britain has to be part of Europe, standing up for British interests but understanding that being a key leading player in Europe is in Britain's interests...for jobs, for investment and for our influence and standing in the world."
The Labour party is favoured to win the next general election which Prime Minister John Major is scheduled to call by May.
Asked if the Toyota's investment will decrease if Britain opts out of the EMU, Okuda, Toyota's top executive, said: "Rather than decreasing the amount, we will leave investments as they are now.
"But if we were to make fresh investments, we would prefer to make them in continental Europe rather than Britain," he added.
Okuda added that Toyota is not currently reviewing its investment strategy in Britain as "everything is still up in air regarding the future of a single European currency".
In other comments on Toyota's overseas plans, company director Hideaki Otaka said the company will take a stake of over 50 percent in a planned joint venture in India.
He said the the company hoped to announce final plans for the venture in the middle of the year, but declined to give any other details, including the size of the investment.

Okuda said the current strength of dollar, which rose to a near-four month high of 122.75 yen in Tokyo on Wednesday, would be more positive for its business than the company had expected, but added that its principle of overseas production will not change.
A weaker yen to the dollar makes Japanese exports to the Unites States more competitive in dollar terms.
Japan's top carmaker also hopes to list on the New York Stock Exchange by the year 2000, he said.
